hand down: give or leave something to people who will live after you
typical: hand sth down (to sb). NOT for: selling.
The ring was handed down from her grandmother.
Stories are handed down by word of mouth.
officially announce a decision, punishment or ruling
typical: hand down a sentence/ruling/verdict. NOT for: asking.
The judge handed down the sentence.
The court handed down its ruling.
hand in: give something to someone in authority
typical: hand sth in, hand in homework/a resignation. NOT for: taking back.
Tom has handed in his resignation.
Did you hand in your homework on time?
hand out: give something to each person in a group
typical: hand sth out (to sb), hand out leaflets/books. NOT for: collecting.
Could you start handing these books out?
He handed out leaflets to the audience.
hand over: give something to someone, especially because they asked for it
typical: hand sth over (to sb), hand over money/the keys. NOT for: keeping.
The soldiers were ordered to hand over their guns.
He handed the phone over to me.
give someone power or responsibility that you used to have
typical: hand sth over to sb, hand over control. NOT for: keeping control.
He handed the business over to his son.
pass to someone in a radio or TV broadcast
typical: hand over to sb. NOT for: ending.
Now I'll hand over to our reporter.
We hand over to Anna for the news.
hang around: wait or spend time somewhere doing nothing (informal)
typical: hang around (a place), hang around for sb. NOT for: working.
I hung around the station for an hour.
spend a lot of time with someone (informal)
typical: hang around with sb. NOT for: avoiding.
He hangs around with older boys.
hang back: stay a short distance away and not go near
typical: hang back (from sb/sth). NOT for: going closer.
He hung back in the shelter of a rock.
not say or do something because you are shy or afraid
typical: hang back from doing sth. NOT for: speaking up.
She hung back from joining in.
hang in: keep trying and not give up (informal, especially AmE)
typical: hang in (there). NOT for: giving up.
Hang in there; it'll get better.
He hung in despite the problems.
hang on: verb
hold something tightly
typical: hang on (to sth), hang on tight. NOT for: letting go.
She hung on to the side of the cart.
Hang on tight!
verb
used to ask someone to wait (spoken)
typical: Hang on!, hang on a minute. NOT for: going.
Hang on! I'll be back in a minute.
Hang on a second.
verb
depend on something
typical: hang on sth. NOT for: being independent.
Everything hangs on the result of this meeting.
The deal hangs on one signature.
verb
continue in a difficult situation
typical: hang on until sth. NOT for: giving up.
We just have to hang on until help comes.
He hung on in the job.
verb
pay close attention to everything someone is saying
typical: hang on sb's every word. NOT for: ignoring.
She watched his face, hanging on his every word.
The audience hung on every word.
hang on to: typical: hang on to sb/sth. NOT for: letting go.
She hung on to my arm.
keep something and not lose or sell it (informal)
typical: hang on to sth. NOT for: getting rid of.
I'll hang on to these old records.
hang out: spend a lot of time in a place or with certain people (informal)
typical: hang out (with sb), hang out at a place. NOT for: working.
I don't know who she hangs out with.
Where do the youngsters hang out?
typical: hang sth out. NOT for: taking down.
My job was to hang out the washing.
Hang the wet things out to dry.
relax and do what you like (let it all hang out)
typical: let it all hang out. NOT for: hiding feelings.
At the party, he let it all hang out.
Relax and let it all hang out.
hang up: typical: hang up (on sb). NOT for: starting a call.
I said goodbye and hung up.
put clothes on a hook or hanger
typical: hang sth up. NOT for: throwing down.
stop doing something (hang up your boots)
typical: hang up your boots/gloves. NOT for: starting.
The footballer hung up his boots.
have on: verb
be wearing a piece of clothing
typical: have (got) sth on. NOT for: taking off.
He had his best suit on.
Jimmy had nothing on but his socks.
verb
have a device switched on
typical: have the TV/radio/heating on. NOT for: switching off.
Billie has the radio on all day long.
Do you have the heating on?
verb
be planning to do something (have sth on)
typical: have sth on tonight/tomorrow. NOT for: being free.
Do you have anything on tonight?
I've got a lot on this week.
verb
trick someone for fun (BrE informal)
typical: be having sb on. NOT for: telling the truth.
You're having me on!
I thought he was having me on.
head for: go in the direction of a place
typical: head for the door/home/town. NOT for: coming from.
be moving towards a situation, usually bad
typical: be heading for trouble/disaster. NOT for: avoiding.
The firm is heading for bankruptcy.
head off: leave to go to another place
typical: head off to + place, I'm heading off. NOT for: arriving.
They headed off to the coast.
typical: head sth off. NOT for: causing.
The President stepped in to head off the conflict.
He tried to head off the problem.
stop someone going somewhere by getting in front of them
typical: head sb off. NOT for: following.
Soldiers headed them off at the border.
head out: leave a place to go somewhere (informal)
typical: head out to + place, head out for the night. NOT for: arriving.
He headed out into the snow.
hear about: be told news or information about someone or something
typical: hear about sb/sth. NOT for: seeing it yourself.
Did you hear about the accident?
know that something exists because you heard it mentioned
typical: hear about sb/sth. NOT for: knowing well.
I've heard about the new cafe.
Have you heard about that school?
hear from: receive news or information from someone
typical: hear from sb. NOT for: hearing about someone.
Do you ever hear from Jack?
I haven't heard from her for ages.
listen to someone give their opinion (in a broadcast)
typical: hear from sb. NOT for: reading.
We hear from some of the victims.
The panel will hear from the minister.
hit back: attack or criticize someone who attacked or criticized you
typical: hit back (at sb), hit back with sth. NOT for: giving in.
The actress hit back at the claims.
United hit back with an equalizer.
hit on: suddenly have an idea or find something by chance
typical: hit on an idea/answer. NOT for: planning.
Then we hit on the idea of asking viewers to donate.
talk to someone in a way that shows you are attracted to them (AmE informal)
typical: hit on sb. NOT for: ignoring.
Dave has hit on most of the women here.
hit up: typical: hit sb up for sth. NOT for: paying.
Did he hit you up for cash again?
She hit me up for a loan.
hold against: continue to dislike someone because of something bad they did in the past
typical: hold sth against sb. NOT for: forgiving.
You can't still hold that against him.
I don't hold it against you.
hold back: verb
stop people or things from moving forward
typical: hold back the crowd/the demonstrators. NOT for: moving forward.
Police held back the crowd.
A barrier held the water back.
verb
stop yourself from showing a feeling
typical: hold back tears/anger/a laugh. NOT for: letting feelings out.
She struggled to hold back her tears.
He couldn't hold back his laughter.
verb
stop someone or something from making progress
typical: hold sb/sth back, be held back by sth. NOT for: helping progress.
The economy is held back by rules.
Shyness held her back at school.
verb
be unwilling to do something, or make someone unwilling
typical: investors hold back, pride held me back. NOT for: moving forward.
Many investors are holding back.
Pride held her back from telling him.
verb
keep something secret
typical: don't hold anything back. NOT for: telling everything.
Tell me everything; don't hold anything back.
He held back some of the facts.
hold off: typical: hold off (on) doing sth. NOT for: hurrying.
Buyers have been holding off until the price falls.
Hold off making your decision until Monday.
prevent someone from attacking, or stop them from coming near
typical: hold sb off. NOT for: letting in.
The guards held off the crowd.
typical: rain holds off. NOT for: starting.
The rain held off until the evening.
I hope the snow holds off.
hold on: verb
wait for a short time, also used on the phone (spoken)
typical: Hold on a minute, can you hold on?. NOT for: holding tightly.
Hold on, I'll just get my coat.
Can you hold on? I'll find her.
verb
used when you have noticed something odd or want to object (spoken)
typical: Hold on! Isn't that ...?. NOT for: waiting politely.
Hold on a minute! That's my car.
Hold on, that's not what you said earlier.
verb
keep your hands tightly around something
typical: hold on tight, hold on to sth. NOT for: waiting.
Hold on tight!
Hold on to my arm.
verb
continue in a difficult situation
typical: hold on until help arrives, hold on to win. NOT for: stopping.
The team held on to win 4-2.
Hold on, the rescue team is nearly here.
hold on to: keep something rather than lose it, sell it or give it away
typical: hold on to sth, hold on to hope. NOT for: giving up.
The soldiers held on to the bridge for three days.
I'll hold on to these records for now.
hold out: verb
stretch out your hand or something you hold
typical: hold out your hand, hold out sth to sb. NOT for: keeping something back.
She held out her hand to greet me.
He held out a cup for some water.
verb
continue to resist or survive
typical: hold out against sb, hold out for days. NOT for: offering something.
The soldiers held out for three weeks.
We can hold out for a while on our food.
verb
offer or give a chance or hope
typical: hold out hope, hold out a chance. NOT for: stretching an arm.
The doctor did not hold out much hope.
The new job holds out a chance of promotion.
verb
last or remain available
typical: supplies hold out, the money holds out. NOT for: resisting an enemy.
I hope the water holds out until we reach the village.
Our supplies didn't hold out very long.
hold over: delay dealing with something until later (formal)
typical: be held over until + time. NOT for: dealing with it now.
The matter was held over for further review.
The meeting was held over until Friday.
use something bad you know about someone to control them
typical: hold sth over sb. NOT for: forgetting.
He knows I've been in prison and holds it over me.
She holds her secret over him.
be shown for longer than planned (a play or film, especially AmE)
typical: be held over. NOT for: closing early.
The show was held over for two more weeks.
hold together: stay united and not separate (a group or organization)
typical: a coalition/family holds together. NOT for: splitting.
The Church held the community together.
typical: hold together, hold sth together. NOT for: falling apart.
The raft held together till we reached shore.
The old car just about held together.
hold up: verb
delay someone or something
typical: be held up, hold up traffic. NOT for: raising something.
We were held up by an accident on the motorway.
The strike held up all the trains.
verb
support something so that it does not fall
typical: hold up a roof, hold up a wall. NOT for: delaying.
Four columns hold up the roof.
He held up the shelf while I fixed it.
verb
rob someone using a weapon
typical: hold up a bank, hold up a shop. NOT for: delaying.
Two men held up the post office yesterday.
The driver was held up at gunpoint.
verb
raise something so people can see it
typical: hold up your hand, hold up a sign. NOT for: supporting something.
Hold up your hand if you know the answer.
She held up the photo for everyone to see.
verb
not become weaker or worse under pressure
typical: hold up well. NOT for: breaking down.
His health has held up well.
The bridge held up in the storm.
hook up: connect a machine to a power supply or other equipment
typical: hook sth up (to sth). NOT for: unplugging.
We hooked the TV up to the cable.
meet someone and become friendly with them, or start a relationship (informal)
typical: hook up with sb. NOT for: avoiding people.
Did you ever hook up with Maisy?
help someone get something they need (informal)
typical: hook sb up with sth. NOT for: refusing.
Can you hook me up with a job?
She hooked him up with tickets.
hunt down: search for someone or something until you find them
typical: hunt sb/sth down. NOT for: letting go.
He hunted down the rare book.
hurry up: used to tell someone to do something more quickly (spoken)
typical: Hurry up!. NOT for: waiting.
typical: hurry sb/sth up. NOT for: delaying.
See if you can hurry things up a little.
